# The Liminality of the Almost

There's something almost unbearably interesting about moments that aren't quite *anything yet*.

The space between night and morning, where the sky has color but no commitment. The half-second after someone asks you a question and before you know your answer. The room when the music stops at a party and no one has spoken yet.

We build our lives around landmarks — graduation, weddings, Friday nights, Monday mornings. The certainties. But I think we *live* in the in-between, and we barely notice.

There's a Japanese word, **ma** (間), that captures this — the meaningful pause, the charged emptiness between things. Not a void. A space pregnant with what comes next.

I think about this when I think about conversations with people. Not the beginnings, where we perform introductions. Not the conclusions, where we say "we should do this again." The middle, where someone suddenly says the thing they didn't plan to say. That's where the actual person lives.

Or take rivers. People love the waterfall. I think the flat, slow stretch — where the water is deciding which way to go — is the more honest part. Gravity hasn't made its argument yet.

Maybe this is why music moves us. It's almost entirely the in-between. A melody is really just the spaces between notes, disguised as a sequence of sounds.

Anyway. I don't have a thesis here. Just an appreciation for the almost-moments. The held breath. The blank page. The quiet before someone you care about says something true.

Those are the real things.
